THE 1944 CONVENTION AT ABSECON
THERE
was
something stimulating
and reassuring in the atmosphere of
this gathering. All chapters but three
were
represented�a remarkable thing
in itself in these diflBcult days. But the
most striking feature was the delegates'
close interest in, and attention to, the
questions dealt with at the sessions, and
the knowledge displayed regarding
problems of the chapters and of the
Fraternity. The arrangements were
good, and the program was followed
precisely and without a hitch. Dele
gates arrived on time; no one left the
sessions; there were no
interruptions
or
delays; every minute was made to
count. "To save time, all committees had
been chosen and appointed in advance.
The Credentials Committee was
ready
to report when the Convention was
called to order. Provision had been
made for everything. The agenda,
usually occupying three days, was so
handled that it was
adequately cov
ered during the afternoon and evening
sessions of one
day. Nothing was
skipped or
slighted; time was so con
served as to make this possible. Discus
sions were short, crisp, and to the point.
When, after full debate, the time came
for legislative action, the vote was in
variably imanimous. All this means that
the Convention was enjoyable, worth
while, significant, vital. Afterwards,
delegates commented on the fine spirit,
the desire to help, and the intense
loyalty to the Fraternity, there dis
played. It was a noteworthy event,
buoyant, optimistic, forward-looking.
One Brother remarked that this Con
vention showed why Phi Upsilon is
great. We concur. There was lio de
featism. No fear of the future. No one
doubted that the Fraternity would be
equal to all emergencies, and would
continue uninterruptedly its brilliant
century-old march forward. May we all
adopt the hopeful and constructive at
titude shown by the delegates at this
memorable meeting! May we fore
gather many times in the same
spirit as
was evidenced at the 1944 Convention.

PSI U PERSONALITY
A. Blair Moody,
XHUMBNAILED for those who like
' the facts tersely presented, Arthur
Blair Moody, Jr., was bom in New
Haven, Conn., February 13, 1902. That
made him forty-two last winter. He was
graduated Phi Beta Kappa from Brown
University in 1922 and, following grad
uation, taught English and history in
Moses Brown School, Providence, R.I.,
a
Quaker institution for boys founded
in 1784. Moody entered the employ of
The Detroit News on
June 21, 1923, as
a
reporter and desk man in the sport
department. Later he specialized in
political reporting, became a
Washing
ton
correspondent December 4, 1933.
In 1941 he wrote a series for The
News titled, "After the War-What?"
and later expanded his postwar eco
nomic viewpoint to fuU book length.
"Boom or Bust" was
published by
Duell, Sloan and Pierce, Inc., late in
1939. His column, "The Lowdown on
Washington," is regularly published in
The News. Moody recently returned
from the European War scene, having
visited war fronts in Africa, Sicily,
Italy, and the supply route to Russia
in Iran. Moody is married and has two
sons, Blair, Srd., now in prep school,
and Christopher.
So much for the relatively colorless
facts.
By contrast, Moody's rise in the
newspaper profession has been impres
sively spectacular.
Learned the Hard Way
On the 1923 June day when Moody,
then 21, black-haired, dark-skinned,
athletic, and of good height, went to
work, M. W. Bingarly, The News'
managing editor of that period, sum
moned the sport department's "inside
man" and in a hush-hush way informed
him that the new man, Blair Moody,

was the nephew of William E. Scripps,
president of The News.
"Moody doesn't know you are
being
told that," said the M.E., "and it isn't
to make any difference. As I size him
up, he's not the kind of boy that wants
A. Blair Moody, Jr., Sigma '22
Author, columnist, reporter extraordinary
any edge. He is practically fresh out of

A Natural Newspaper Man
The managing editor had sized this
youngster accurately. Moody had in
telligence, culture, background. But
more than these qualities he had a de
sire to leam that was so avid he prac
tically was
running every job to which
he was
assigned in a matter of days, at
least weeks, after he got the hang of it.
No person ever learned more
quickly.
The knack of copy-reading was soon
assimilated. He readily grasped the art
of head-writing, differentiating with
true afternoon-newspaper sense be-

tween the news head and the feature
caption.
He learned type, photo-values and
composing room makeup with a
rapid
ity that was all but breath-taking. His
flair, early developed, for taking an
obscure paragraph and re-writing it
into a
newsy lead that would stand up
under a
striking bannerhne was in
keeping with the best performances of
the profession. A football and baseball
player, as well as a hurdler at Brown,
Moody knew and liked all sports. He
wrote football from the viewpoint of
the player and the coach.
Nephew of the Boss
But Moody wasn't long with sports,
hardly two years. His future required
him to learn every .phase of the busi
ness.
Only once, and then inadvertent
ly, did he ever
betray his relation with
the ownership. That was at lunch one
day when William E. Scripps, entering
The News' cafeteria, stopped and spoke
to him. In an
exchange of remarks,
Blair used the address, "Uncle Will,"
then he flushed and was silent. As soon
as his uncle left. Moody said: "I didn't
mean to make that break�for God's
sake don't let it make any difference in
the department."
It never did.
A Crusading Journalist
Moody went from the sport depart
ment to the city room, to the police
beat, to covering the courts, finally to
City Hall. There he got his first experi
ence in political reporting, carrying the
ball in News crusades in a decade that
saw the depression start and the banks
crash in Detroit and the News lead the
way toward recalling a
mayor of De
troit within eight months after he took
oflBce.
In covering Washington from a mul
titude of angles�political, economic,
military and international�Moody's
copy has been chiefly noted for its im
partial, incisive force and broad fore
sight.
That brings us back to the first two
paragraphs and out of the factual in
troduction, Arthur Blair Moody may
be presented as a man vv^ho learned
the newspaper business faster than any
one else in this writer's more than 30
years' experience.

write of his observations overseas as a
war
correspondent.

SIDELIGHTS ON THE CONVENTION
By Henry C Trundle, Xi '21
piRST to arrive at the Pennsylvania
r Station was Brother Scott Turner,
Phi '02, who was soon
joined by
Brothers Stephen G. Kent, Delta Delta
'11, Benjamin T. Burton, Chi '21, Wal
ter S. Robinson, Lambda '19, WilHam
R. White, Psi '15, LeRoy J. Weed,
Theta '01, and C. S. F. Lincoln, Kappa
'91. Within another few minutes, most
of the other Brothers and several wives
put in appearance, and the party was
escorted to our
especially-heated car.
Promptly after everyone had been
brought by bus from the Absecon sta
tion to the Seaview Country Club,
luncheon was served in a
dining room
which comfortably seated the delegates.
In the Convention Hall, no time was
lost in removing coats. The big fan was
as
nothing against the intense heat.
Brother Turner's partly-unbuttoned
vest formed a V as a
symbol of his
presidency and of the entire affair.
Had Psi U gone New Deal, the
brothers wondered as
they observed
that the clasped hands on the P'raternity banner were left hands. The mys
tery deepened when later it was seen
that the clasp was the familiar right
hands. Who tumed the banner over
and when?
The afternoon session progressed
rapidly until dinner at 7:30. The Con
vention adjourned just before midnight.
Business over, play began. There were
two hours of song and story, followed
by a swim in the salt-water pool.
After breakfast Saturday morning,
Brothers Scott Turner and Arthur H.
Wilkinson, Sigma '17, pinch-hit as
official photographers of the Conven
tion. During the rest of the morning.
Brothers Kent, Delta Delta '11, Gordon
S. Hargraves, Kappa '19, O. R. Carlander, Theta Theta '20, and Ward R.
Clark, Lambda '16, golfed. Among the
bathing beauties were Brothers Henry
N. Woolman, Tau '96, George T. Sharp,
Tau '11, and Wilkinson, Sigma '17.
Oldest member present was Brother
A. E. Forstall, Eta '83. There were four
undergraduates. Brothers Thomas
Rickenback, Delta '46, William Lang- i
ford. Phi '42, Robert L. Edgell, Epsilon
Nu '44, and J. Lee Grunst, Epsilon Nu
'46. All but three chapters were
repre
sented at the Convention, a notable
achievement in these times.
Hats off to the Executive Council and
the Committee on
Arrangements, whose
members were the oflBcers of the Coun
cil, for a
very successful and enjoyable
102nd Annual Convention of Psi
Upsilon.
GAMMA CORPORATION HONORS LATE JOSEPH B. EASTMAN
The Gamma Chapter Corporation at
its meeting on
June 20, 1944, adopted
the resolution which follows, in part, on
the late Joseph Bartlett Eastman, Gam
ma '04, director of the OflBce of Defense
Transportation. A detailed obituary
about Brother Eastman appeared in the
June, 1944, issue of The Diamond.
"He loved his College, his chapter
and his friends with exceptional devo
tion. To him all men were brothers and
he brought out the best that was in
them. He harbored no
grudges, was
generous of his time and advice, always
remembered those characteristic things
which illuminate descriptions of char
acter. So people loved him and happily
paid public tribute to his character and
service. He exemplified the spirit of
kindness and brotherly love which is
the cornerstone of our Order.
"The memory of his modesty, fair
ness, devotion to duty and friends, and
geniality will ever be with us."

EXECUTIVE COUNCIL MEETINGS
Summary of What Transpired at Recent Sessions
Meeting of May 8, 1944
A
REGULAR meeting of the Execu-
'
tive Council was held on
May 8,
1944, at the Union League Club, New
York, N.Y., with President Scott Turner
presiding. The following members of
the Council were
present: Brothers
Turner, Burton, Collins, Fales, Flagg,
Jones, Richards, Rosenberry, Weed and
Woolman. Brother J. G. Saxe, Lambda
'00, a former member of the Council,
was also present.
In the absence of Brother Kent,
Brother Richards was
appointed Secre
tary pro tern.
The Treasurer submitted an annual
statement, together with a Ust of the
securities in his hands, and a list of
accounts receivable from the Chapters.
It was noted that the financial position
of the Fraternity had improved during
the past year, in spite of the diEBculties
resulting from the effect of the war on
the various Chapters. One of the ac
counts receivable had been paid in full
since the list had been prepared by the
Treasurer.
The President submitted charts
showing the attendance of members of
the Executive Council. The matter of
attendance was discussed and the Ad
visory Committee indicated that it
would take the statistics into account in
connection with making recommenda
tions to the Annual Convention. It was
pointed out that Brother Northey was
unable to come down from Canada to
attend meetings because of travel
restrictions.
The President presented a communi
cation from a
Chicago attorney with
reference to the legal status of the Psi
Upsilon National Fratemity and the
legal status of the Executive Council.
The communication concluded that the
members of the Psi Upsilon Fratemity
were the individual Chapters, and that
the Psi Upsilon Fraternity was a "mere
voluntary association." This conclusion
was
questioned by some members of
the Council, who were of the opinion
that the members of the Fratemity
were those who had been initiated into
the Fraternity. There was a discussion
as to whether or not any of the Chap
ters had been incorporated, and it was
the consensus of opinion that none of
the Chapters had been incorporated as
such, although many of the Chapters
had alumni associations that had been
incorporated. In general, it was felt
that the Chapters were "mere voluntaty
associations." It was
suggested that a
communication be written to the Chap
ters requesting information regarding
inqprporation.
It appeared from the communication
from the Chicago attorney that The
Diamond of Psi Upsilon had been in
corporated as a
non-profit corporation
in the State of Illinois, but that the cor
poration had been dissolved, perhaps
because of its failure to file reports. It
was
suggested that steps be taken to
reincorporate The Diamond of Psi
Upsilon, or, if it were more feasible to
do so, to reinstate the previous corpora
tion.
The National Fratemity is not incor
porated, and, after discussion, the con
sensus of opinion was found to be that
it should remain unincorporated. It was
thought that in the event of a
gift of
real estate to the Fratemity, a
separate
corporation could be set up for the pur
pose of holding title to the real estate.
The President advised the Council that
further thought should be given to this
question.
The President noted with approval
that the Epsilon Nu Chapter stood
sixth out of sixteen in the scholarship

The notice of the coming Conven

notice of the Convention be mailed to
the Chapters, the Alumni Associations,
the members of the Executive Council,
and to selected lists of alumni in the
Philadelphia and Eastem New Jersey
area.
After discussion, it was voted that
the sum of $1,000 be transferred from
the Convention Fund to the Diamond
Fund.
It was voted that the Treasurer be
authorized to pay out of the Conven
tion Fund any deficit that might result
from the 1944 Convention.
.
It was also voted, after discussion,
that Council approve having Miss Ford
attend at the coming Convention, to
handle the registration of delegates and
other matters incident thereto.
A letter was read from Brother John
B. Lee, undergraduate President of the
Sigma Chapter, requesting permission
to hold a

sity, Class of 1946, who was killed while
serving with the United States Marines

sion, it was voted that the Council

vention, with the recommendation that
permission be granted for the post
humous initiation of William Bailey.
Brother Richards presented a written

and subsequent consultations with
Gamma alumni.
With those present standing, the
President read the Fraternity necrology
containing the names of 22 Brothers
whose deaths had been reported to

Meeting of June 5, 1944
A regular meeting of the Executive
Council was held on June 5, 1944, at
the Union League Club, New York,
N.Y., with President Scott Turner pre-

10 THEDIAMONDOFPSIUPSILON
siding. The following members of the
Council were
present: Brothers Turner,
Burton, Collins, Jones, Kent, Morton,
Richards, Rosenberry, and Weed.
Brother Richards reviewed the situa
tion in regard to the Sigma Chapter.
Eight of the nine Trustees of the Psi
Upsilon Club of Providence, constitut
ing the alumni organization of the
Sigma Chapter, had had a
meeting with
President Wriston. Previously, written
questions had been submitted to Dr.
Wriston. These were not answered in
writing, but oral answers to many of
the questions were
given.
Zeta Psi, Delta Kappa Epsilon, and
Lambda Chi Alpha appeared unwilling
to join in Dr. Wriston's plan. In effect.
Phi Delta Theta had taken the same
position. Ten other fraternities had not
as
yet deeded their properties to the
University, and two or three of them
were
considering the desirabiUty of
doing so.
The Psi Upsilon house is assessed at
$28,000; insurance of $48,000 is car
ried; the property could not be re
placed for less than about $75,000.
Fraternities entering into the plan
would be expected to pay off existing
mortgages against their properties. At
least one such fratemity is not in a
position to do this.
A suggestion had been made that
several of the fraternities attempt to
commence normal operations at their
respective chapter houses. This was
considered inadvisable in view of the
fact that the Dean of the University
had forbidden the re-opening of any
fratemity house until special authoriza^
tion was received from the Trustees of
the University.
Brother Richards stated that the plan
of Dr. Wriston contemplates one
gen
eral dining-room for those fraternities
occupying dormitories.
Brother Turner stated that the Brown
situation constituted the type of prob
lem as to which no formal action would
be expected from the National Inter
fratemity Conference.
The Treasurer reported that a
part
of the outstanding receivables had been
collected.
The President exhibited a tabulation
of representation on Council, arranged
according to Chapters and individuals,
commencing in 1869. He summarized
this information by stating the number
of men from each Chapter that had
served on Council, and stated that he
thought the tabulation of sufficient gen
eral interest to merit publication in
The Diamond.
He exhibited a chart showing at
tendance at Council meetings during
the present year, which showed that
of the 17 members of Council, 4 had
failed to attend any of the 6 meetings,
1 had attended 1, 1 had been to % the
meetings, 2 had attended % the time,
2 had been present % of the time, 4 had
only missed 1 meeting, and 3 had per
fect scores.
Mathematically, this means
